{{Short description|Identity for a sequence of orthogonal polynomials}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Christoffel–Darboux formula''' or '''Christoffel–Darboux theorem''' is an identity for a sequence of [[orthogonal polynomials]], introduced by {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Elwin Bruno Christoffel|first=Elwin Bruno|last= Christoffel|year=1858}} and {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Jean Gaston Darboux|first=Jean Gaston|last= Darboux|year=1878}}.

{{Math theorem
| name = Christoffel–Darboux formula
| note = 
| math_statement = if a sequence of polynomials <math>f_0, f_1, \dots</math> are of degrees <math>0, 1, \dots</math>, and orthogonal with respect to a probability measure <math>\mu</math>, then

:<math>\sum_{j=0}^n \frac{f_j(x) f_j(y)}{h_j} = \frac{k_n}{h_n k_{n+1}} \frac{f_n(y) f_{n+1}(x) - f_{n+1}(y) f_n(x)}{x - y}</math>

where <math>h_j = \|f_j\|^2_\mu</math> are the squared norms, and <math>k_j</math> are the leading coefficients.
}}

There is also a "confluent form" of this identity by taking <math>y\to x</math> limit:

{{Math theorem
| name = Christoffel–Darboux formula, confluent form
| note = 
| math_statement = <math display=block>  \sum_{j=0}^n \frac{f_j^2(x)}{h_j} = \frac{k_n}{h_n k_{n+1}} \left[f_{n + 1}'(x)f_{n}(x) - f_{n}'(x) f_{n + 1}(x)\right].</math>
}}

== Proof ==

{{Math theorem|name=Lemma|note=|math_statement=

Let <math>p_n</math> be a sequence of polynomials orthonormal with respect to a probability measure <math>\mu</math>, such that <math>p_n</math> has degree <math>n</math>, and define<math display="block">a_{n}=\langle x p_{n},p_{n+1}\rangle,\qquad b_{n}=\langle x p_{n},p_{n}\rangle,\qquad n\geq0</math>(they are called the "Jacobi parameters"), then we have the three-term recurrence<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Świderski |first1=Grzegorz |last2=Trojan |first2=Bartosz |date=2021-08-01 |title=Asymptotic Behaviour of Christoffel–Darboux Kernel Via Three-Term Recurrence Relation I |journal=Constructive Approximation |language=en |volume=54 |issue=1 |pages=49–116 |doi=10.1007/s00365-020-09519-w |s2cid=202677666 |issn=1432-0940|doi-access=free |arxiv=1909.09107 }}</ref><math display="block">\begin{array}{l l}{{p_{0}(x)=1,\qquad p_{1}(x)=\frac{x-b_{0}}{a_{0}},}}\\ {{x p_{n}(x)=a_{n}p_{n+1}(x)+b_{n}p_{n}(x)+a_{n-1}p_{n-1}(x),\qquad n\geq1}}\end{array}</math>
}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof= 
By definition, <math>\langle xp_n, p_k \rangle = \langle p_n, xp_k \rangle</math>, so if <math>k \leq n-2</math>, then <math>xp_k</math> is a linear combination of <math>p_0, ..., p_{n-1}</math>, and thus <math>\langle xp_n, p_k \rangle = 0</math>. So, to construct <math>p_{n+1}</math>, it suffices to perform Gram-Schmidt process on <math>xp_n</math> using <math>p_{n}, p_{n-1}</math>, which yields the desired recurrence.
}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof of Christoffel–Darboux formula|proof=

For any sequence of nonzero constants <math>c_0, c_1, \dots</math>, we can change each <math>f_k</math> to <math>c_kf_k</math>, and both sides of the equation would remain unchanged. Thus WLOG, scale each <math>f_n</math> to <math>p_n</math>.

Since <math>\frac{k_{n+1}}{k_n}xp_n - p_{n+1}</math> is a degree <math>n</math> polynomial, it is perpendicular to <math>p_{n+1}</math>, and so <math>\langle \frac{k_{n+1}}{k_n}xp_n, p_{n+1}\rangle = \langle p_{n+1}, p_{n+1}\rangle = 1</math>. Thus, <math display="inline">a_n=\frac{k_n}{k_{n+1}}</math>.

Base case:

<math display="block">\frac{k_0}{k_1} \frac{p_0(y) p_1(x)-p_1(y) p_0(x)}{x-y}=\frac{k_0}{k_1} \frac{p_0(y) \frac{x-b_0}{a_0}-p_0(x) \frac{y-b_0}{a_0}}{x-y} = 1</math>

Induction:

<math display="block">
\begin{aligned}
&(x-y) \sum_{j=0}^n p_j(x) p_j(y)=(x-y) \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} p_j(x) p_j(y)+p_n(x) p_n(y)(x-y) \\
& \stackrel{\text { (IH) }}{=} \frac{k_{n-1}}{k_n}\left[p_n(x) p_{n-1}(y)-p_n(y) p_{n-1}(x)\right] + (x-y)p_n(x) p_n(y)
\end{aligned}
</math>

By the three-term recurrence,

<math display="block">
\begin{aligned}
& x p_n(x)=a_n p_{n+1}(x)+b_n p_n(x)+a_{n-1} p_{n-1}(x) \\
& y p_n(y)=a_n p_{n+1}(y)+b_n p_n(y)+a_{n-1} p_{n-1}(y)
\end{aligned}
</math>

Multiply the first by <math display="inline">p_n(y)</math> and the second by <math display="inline">p_n(x)</math> and subtract:

<math display="block">
(x-y) p_n(x) p_n(y)=a_n\left[p_n(y) p_{n+1}(x)-p_n(x) p_{n+1}(y)\right]+a_{n-1}\left[p_n(y) p_{n-1}(x)-p_n(x) p_{n-1}(y)\right]
</math>

Now substitute in <math display="inline">a_n=\frac{k_n}{k_{n+1}}, \quad a_{n-1}=\frac{k_{n-1}}{k_n}</math> and simplify.
}}

==Specific cases==

=== Hermite ===
The [[Hermite polynomials]] are orthogonal with respect to the gaussian distribution.

The <math>H</math> polynomials are orthogonal with respect to <math>\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} e^{- x^2}</math>, and with <math>k_n = 2^n</math>.<math display="block">\sum_{k=0}^n \frac{H_k(x) H_k(y)}{k!2^k} = \frac{1}{n!2^{n+1}}\,\frac{H_n(y) H_{n+1}(x) - H_n(x) H_{n+1}(y)}{x - y}.</math>The <math>\operatorname{He}</math> polynomials are orthogonal with respect to <math>\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac 12 x^2}</math>, and with <math>k_n = 1</math>.<math display="block">\sum_{k=0}^n \frac{\operatorname{He}_k(x) \operatorname{He}_k(y)}{k!} = \frac{1}{n!}\,\frac{\operatorname{He}_n(y) \operatorname{He}_{n+1}(x) - \operatorname{He}_n(x) \operatorname{He}_{n+1}(y)}{x - y}.</math>The confluent form and the three-term recurrence gives<math display="block">\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{H_k(x)^2}{k!2^k}=\frac{H_{n+1}(x)^2-H_{n+2}(x)H_n(x)}{n!2^{n+1}}</math><math display="block">\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{\operatorname{He}_k(x)^2}{k!}=\frac{\operatorname{He}_{n+1}(x)^2-\operatorname{He}_{n+2}(x)\operatorname{He}_n(x)}{n!}</math>

=== Laguerre ===
The [[Laguerre polynomials]] <math>L_n</math> are orthonormal with respect to the [[exponential distribution]] <math>e^{-x}, \quad x \in (0, \infty)</math>, with <math>k_n = (-1)^n/n!</math>, so<math display="block">\sum_{k=0}^n L_k(x) L_k(y)=\frac{n+1}{x-y}\left[L_n(x) L_{n+1}(y)-L_n(y) L_{n+1}(x)\right]</math>

=== Legendre ===
[[Associated Legendre polynomials]]:

: <math>\begin{align} (\mu-\mu')\sum_{l=m}^L\,(2l+1)\frac{(l-m)!}{(l+m)!}\,P_{lm}(\mu)P_{lm}(\mu')=\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\\\frac{(L-m+1)!}{(L+m)!}\big[P_{L+1\,m}(\mu)P_{Lm}(\mu')-P_{Lm}(\mu)P_{L+1\,m}(\mu')\big].\end{align}</math>

== Christoffel–Darboux kernel ==
The summation involved in the Christoffel–Darboux formula is invariant by scaling the polynomials with nonzero constants. Thus, each [[probability distribution]] <math>\mu</math> defines a series of functions<math display="block">K_n(x,y) := \sum_{j=0}^n f_j(x) f_j(y)/h_j, \quad n = 0, 1, \dots</math>which are called the '''Christoffel–Darboux kernels'''. By the orthogonality, the kernel satisfies <math display="block">\int f(y) K_n(x, y) \mathrm{d} \mu(y)= \begin{cases}f(x), & f \in \operatorname{Span}\left(p_0, p_1, \ldots, p_n\right) \\ 0, & \int_a^b f(x) p_{\ell}(x) \mathrm{d} \mu(x)=0(\ell=0,1, \ldots, n)\end{cases}</math>In other words, the kernel is an [[integral operator]] that orthogonally projects each polynomial to the space of polynomials of degree up to <math>n</math>.
